listeningParts.title: Booking a family visit to a castle
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones the visitor bookings office of a historic castle to plan a family day out.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Hawksmoor Castle visitor bookings, Rachel speaking. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I'm hoping to book a visit for my family during the school holidays. We'd like to do one of your guided tours, if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. How many people would that be?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Two adults and three children. The children are six, nine and thirteen.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. Our standard ticket gives you entry to the castle, the gardens and the exhibition in the old stables. Adult tickets are fourteen pounds fifty, and children aged five to sixteen are seven pounds. But we also have a family ticket for two adults and up to three children, which is forty pounds, so that would be the best value for you.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Great, the family ticket, then. And what about the tours?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There are two. The Castle Highlights tour lasts about an hour and covers the great hall, the chapel and the medieval kitchens. Then there's the Hidden Castle tour, which takes you into parts of the building that are normally closed to the public, including the dungeon and the top of the north tower. That one lasts ninety minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The Hidden Castle tour sounds exciting. Is it suitable for children?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It is, but there's a minimum age of eight, because there are a lot of narrow stone staircases. There are a hundred and twelve steps up to the top of the tower alone.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ah. My youngest is only six.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Then I'd suggest the Highlights tour for the whole family. And if your older two would like something extra, they could join our archaeology workshop in the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: What happens in that?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's run by our education team in the old dairy, next to the walled garden. The children learn how archaeologists work, and they get to handle real objects found during excavations here at the castle, such as pieces of pottery and old coins. It lasts two hours and costs six pounds per child. It's designed for ages nine to fourteen, so both of your older children could take part.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect, they'd love that. Which days does it run?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: During the holidays it's on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Which date were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We were hoping for Thursday the twenty-third of August.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Let me have a look. I'm afraid the workshop on the twenty-third is already full, but there are still places on Tuesday the twenty-eighth.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The twenty-eighth would work too. We're staying in the area that whole week.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good. On that day, the Highlights tours start at ten thirty, twelve o'clock and half past two. The workshop begins at two, so I'd recommend the first tour of the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Ten thirty, then. That gives us time for lunch in between. Is there somewhere to eat?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's a café in the courtyard that serves hot meals and sandwiches, or you're very welcome to bring your own food. The picnic area is down by the lake, and there are tables there.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'll probably bring a picnic. What about parking?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Parking is free for visitors. The main car park is closest to the entrance, but it's usually full by about eleven in the holidays, so if you arrive for the ten thirty tour you should be fine. Otherwise there's an overflow car park, which is about ten minutes' walk away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I book everything now?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes. Could I have your name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Mark Treloar. T-R-E-L-O-A-R.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Treloar. And a contact phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's oh-seven-seven-one-three, four-eight-two, nine-six-oh.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. So that's a family ticket at forty pounds, plus two places on the workshop at six pounds each, which makes fifty-two pounds altogether. The Highlights tour is included in the ticket price, so there's no extra charge for that.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very reasonable. Is there anything else we need to know?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: I'll send you a confirmation email. Please show it at the gatehouse when you arrive, and the staff there will give you wristbands. The children will need to wear theirs for the workshop. Oh, and the castle floors can be uneven, so I'd recommend comfortable shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Will do. Can we bring our dog?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Dogs are welcome in the gardens and the picnic area if they're on a lead, but not inside the castle buildings, I'm afraid, apart from assistance dogs.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Thanks very much for your help, Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: You're welcome. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: Training new volunteer guides
listeningParts.contextDescription: The volunteer manager of a historic country house gives a talk to new volunteer room guides.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you all for coming. My name's Helen Marsh, and I'm the volunteer manager here at Ashcombe Hall. Before you start shadowing our experienced guides next week, I'd like to give you a bit of background about the house and explain what we'll be asking you to do.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: First, a little history. The hall was built in the early seventeenth century for a wealthy wool merchant, and the same family lived here for more than three hundred years. After the Second World War, the family could no longer afford to repair the roof, and the government was asking them to pay very heavy taxes on the estate. So, rather than sell it to a developer, they gave the house and its contents to our heritage trust. That's why so much of the original furniture is still here, which is quite unusual for a house of this age.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, many of you have told me you volunteered because you love history, and that's wonderful. But when I ask our long-serving volunteers what they enjoy most, they rarely mention the history. What they talk about is the conversations they have with visitors, and the feeling that they're helping people to connect with the house. So please don't worry about memorising every date. Visitors would much rather hear a good story than a list of facts.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Let me say a word about conservation, because it affects almost everything we do. You'll notice that many of the rooms are quite dark, and that the curtains are often partly closed. Visitors sometimes complain about this, so you need to be able to explain it. Light, and especially the ultraviolet part of sunlight, causes permanent damage to textiles, paintings and paper. Colours fade, and fabrics become weak and split. Once that damage is done, it can't be reversed, so keeping light levels low is the best way of protecting the collection.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: On photography, our policy has changed recently. Visitors may now take photographs in all the rooms, but they must not use flash, and tripods and selfie sticks aren't allowed, because they're too easy to knock against objects. If you see somebody touching furniture or a painting, please don't shout at them. Most people simply don't realise that the oils and salts on our skin can damage surfaces. Just explain politely why we ask people not to touch.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Now, let me tell you about some of the rooms you'll be working in, so you know what to expect. The Great Hall is the first room visitors see, and it's usually the busiest. It's also where you'll find the oldest object in the house, a carved oak chest that's actually older than the building itself; the family brought it with them from their previous home.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The Library is much quieter. It contains around four thousand books, and it's the room where visitors most often ask questions we can't answer. That's fine. There's a folder of information in a drawer of the desk, and if that doesn't help, write the question down and we'll find out.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: In the Long Gallery upstairs, we have a dressing-up box with copies of seventeenth-century clothes, and children, and quite a few adults, can try them on. It gets noisy, so it's a good room for volunteers who enjoy working with families.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: The Kitchen is one of the most popular rooms. Every Sunday, one of our volunteers bakes bread there using a historic recipe, and visitors can taste it. If you're interested in helping with that, let me know, because you'll need a food hygiene certificate first.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: And finally, the Chapel. It's the smallest room open to the public, and because of the stone floor it's always cold, so please bring a warm layer if you're on duty there. It's also the room where the stained-glass windows are, and they're the reason we're raising money at the moment, as two of them need urgent repair.

dialogue.speaker: Manager
dialogue.text: Right, I'll hand out your uniforms and name badges now, and then we'll walk round the house together.

listeningParts.title: A visitor survey in a World Heritage city
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two tourism students, Owen and Grace, discuss their visitor survey in the city of Bath with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've finished collecting the data for your survey in Bath. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. As you know, we wanted to find out what visitors think about crowding in the city centre, and whether it affects how much they enjoy their visit. Bath's been a World Heritage Site since 1987, and it's one of the few places where the whole city is included, not just a single monument, so it seemed like a good case.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And how did you collect your responses?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: We did face-to-face questionnaires at four locations: outside the Roman Baths, near the Abbey, in the Royal Crescent and at the railway station. We'd originally planned to use an online survey with a QR code on posters, but in our pilot week almost nobody scanned it, so we changed our approach.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a useful thing to mention in your methodology. How many people did you speak to?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Two hundred and forty in total. We'd hoped for three hundred, but it rained heavily on two of our survey days, and there were far fewer people about.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Two hundred and forty is still a reasonable sample for a project of this size. Did you have any trouble persuading people to take part?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Not really. We kept the questionnaire short, about five minutes, and we told people that at the start. Families with young children were the hardest to stop, understandably, and some tour groups couldn't take part because their guides were keeping them on a strict schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's worth noting, because it means certain types of visitor may be under-represented. What were your main findings?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: The most interesting one was the difference between day visitors and people staying overnight. Day visitors were much more likely to say the city felt overcrowded. We think that's partly because they all tend to visit the same few places at the same times, usually between eleven and three.

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Whereas people staying in the city could go to the Roman Baths early in the morning or in the evening, when it's much quieter. Several of them told us that the evening was the best part of their visit.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That fits with what other research has found. Did the crowding actually reduce people's enjoyment?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Less than we expected. Most people said the crowds were annoying, but they still gave their overall visit a high score. The thing that bothered them more was the lack of information about less famous sights. A lot of visitors didn't know there was anything to see beyond the main attractions.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point, because spreading visitors around is one of the main strategies that heritage cities use. Did anyone suggest what might help?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Quite a few people mentioned a phone app with suggested walking routes. And some older visitors said they'd prefer a simple printed map, because they didn't want to keep looking at their phones.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So you could recommend both. What about residents? Did you speak to any?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: Only a few, by accident, really. Some people we stopped turned out to live in Bath, and they had very strong opinions, mostly about coach parking and noise. We didn't include them in the main results, because our questionnaire was designed for visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd mention them in your discussion as a possible area for further research, rather than ignoring them completely. Residents' views are central to the debate about tourism in historic cities. Now, what's the biggest weakness of your study, do you think?

dialogue.speaker: Owen
dialogue.text: Probably the timing. We only collected data in October, which isn't the busiest season. In August the results might be quite different.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Make that clear, and be careful not to claim that your findings apply all year round. Right, what are your next steps?

dialogue.speaker: Grace
dialogue.text: We're going to enter all the data into a spreadsheet this week, and then make some charts comparing the four locations.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And include a photograph of each location, so that readers can picture them. I'd like a complete draft by the twelfth of December, please.

listeningParts.title: Intangible cultural heritage
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a heritage studies course about the protection of living traditions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. So far in this course, we've mainly been talking about heritage you can touch: buildings, monuments and landscapes. Today I want to turn to a different kind of heritage, which UNESCO calls intangible cultural heritage. In simple terms, this means living traditions: the practices, skills and knowledge that communities pass from one generation to the next.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For a long time, international heritage protection focused almost entirely on physical sites. The World Heritage Convention of 1972, which we discussed last week, was designed to protect monuments and natural areas. But many countries, particularly in Asia, Africa and Latin America, argued that this approach favoured nations with grand stone buildings, and ignored the heritage that mattered most to their own people, such as music, festivals and oral traditions.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One country had in fact been protecting living traditions for decades. In 1950, Japan passed a law that covered not only objects and buildings but also performing arts and craft skills. A few years later, it began recognising individual masters of traditional arts, such as pottery, puppet theatre and sword-making, as what are popularly known as Living National Treasures. The idea was that the skill itself was the treasure, and that the people who held it should be supported so that they could train apprentices.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: At the international level, an important step came from an unexpected place: a market square in Marrakesh, in Morocco. The square, called Jemaa el-Fnaa, is famous for its storytellers, musicians and other performers. In the 1990s, there were plans to develop the area, and the Spanish writer Juan Goytisolo, who lived in the city, campaigned to protect not just the square as a space, but the activities that took place there. In 2001, it was among the first examples to be recognised in a new UNESCO programme for oral and intangible heritage.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This eventually led to the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, which was adopted in 2003 and came into force three years later. You'll notice that it uses the word safeguarding rather than protection. That's deliberate. A building can be protected by preventing change, but a living tradition must be allowed to change, or it dies. The aim is to make sure the tradition continues to be practised and passed on.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The convention identifies five broad areas. The first is oral traditions, including language as a means of passing them on. The second is the performing arts, such as music, dance and theatre. Third, there are social practices, rituals and festive events. Fourth, knowledge and practices concerning nature, for example traditional medicine or methods of navigation. And fifth, traditional craftsmanship.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Countries can nominate elements for a Representative List, and there's also a separate list for traditions that are in urgent need of safeguarding, often because there are very few practitioners left. Food is a particularly popular category. The French gastronomic meal was inscribed in 2010, and in 2017 the art of the Neapolitan pizza maker was added. In 2020, four North African countries, Algeria, Mauritania, Morocco and Tunisia, made a joint nomination for the knowledge and practices of making and eating couscous, which was seen as a good example of countries sharing a tradition rather than competing over it.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, the system isn't without its critics. One concern is that once a tradition is listed, there may be pressure to perform it in a fixed, official version for tourists, which can freeze something that has always varied from village to village. Another is commercialisation: a listed festival or dish can become a marketing brand. And some anthropologists ask a difficult question: who has the right to decide what a community's authentic tradition is? Is it the government, experts, or the community itself?

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There's also the question of what happens when a tradition is shared across borders. Several nominations have caused disagreements between neighbouring countries, each claiming a dish, a dance or a musical instrument as its own. That's one reason why joint nominations, like the couscous example, are increasingly encouraged.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For your next seminar, I'd like you to choose one listed element and investigate how listing has affected the community that practises it.

readingPassages.title: The temples that moved
paragraphs: On the west bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, close to the border with Sudan, stand two of the most extraordinary monuments of the ancient world. The temples of Abu Simbel were cut directly into a sandstone cliff during the reign of the pharaoh Ramesses II, in the thirteenth century BC. The larger of the two is guarded by four colossal seated statues of the king, each around twenty metres high. The smaller temple was dedicated to his principal wife, Nefertari, and to the goddess Hathor. Yet the temples visitors see today are not where Ramesses' builders left them. In the 1960s, they were cut into pieces and moved to higher ground.

For many centuries after the decline of ancient Egypt, the temples were largely forgotten, and sand from the desert gradually buried much of the larger one. In 1813, the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt saw the tops of the great statues emerging from the sand. Four years later, the Italian explorer Giovanni Belzoni cleared enough of the entrance to get inside. European visitors who followed were amazed by the scale of the carvings and by the wall reliefs inside, which show scenes from Ramesses' military campaigns, including the famous Battle of Kadesh.

The threat to the temples came in the twentieth century. In the 1950s, the Egyptian government decided to build a new, much larger dam on the Nile at Aswan, to control the river's annual flood, store water for farming and generate electricity. The Aswan High Dam would create an enormous reservoir, later named Lake Nasser, stretching hundreds of kilometres south into Sudan. The rising water would cover a large part of the region known as Nubia, forcing tens of thousands of people to leave their homes, and it would drown dozens of ancient sites, including Abu Simbel.

In 1959, Egypt and Sudan asked UNESCO for help, and the following year the organisation launched an international appeal to save the monuments of Nubia. The response was remarkable. Around fifty countries contributed money or expertise, and archaeologists from many nations hurried to excavate and record sites before they disappeared under the water. Several temples were dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere, and a number were given to countries that had supported the campaign. The Temple of Dendur, for example, was given to the United States and now stands in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Abu Simbel presented the greatest challenge of all. Various solutions were proposed, including surrounding the temples with a huge dam of their own, or lifting each temple in a single piece using hydraulic jacks. In the end, engineers chose a plan that was cheaper and less risky. Work began in 1964, while a temporary barrier held back the rising water. The temples were cut into more than a thousand blocks, many of which weighed around twenty tonnes. Workers used hand saws for the most delicate cuts, so that the faces of the statues would not be damaged, and the blocks were numbered so that they could be put back in exactly the right order.

The blocks were then reassembled on a site about sixty-five metres higher and around two hundred metres further from the river. Because the original temples had been carved into a natural cliff, the engineers also had to recreate the cliff. They built two huge concrete domes over the reconstructed temples and covered them with rock and sand, so that from the outside the site looks much as it did before. The project was completed in 1968, and the total cost was around forty million US dollars, a very large sum at that time.

One feature of the temples raised a particular concern. The larger temple was aligned so that, on two days each year, in February and October, the rising sun shines along the entire length of the building and lights up statues in the inner sanctuary, around sixty metres from the entrance. Interestingly, one of the four statues, representing Ptah, a god associated with the underworld, always remains in shadow. The engineers worked hard to keep this alignment in the new location, and they largely succeeded, although the event is now thought to occur about a day later than it did originally.

The Nubian campaign had consequences far beyond Egypt. It showed that the world's nations were willing to share responsibility for protecting sites of exceptional importance, wherever they happened to be. This idea helped to shape the World Heritage Convention, adopted by UNESCO in 1972, under which countries agree to identify and protect places of outstanding universal value. In 1979, Abu Simbel and the other Nubian monuments were themselves added to the World Heritage List. Today, hundreds of thousands of tourists visit the temples each year, many of them arriving by plane or coach from Aswan, about two hundred and eighty kilometres to the north.

readingPassages.title: Loved to death: protecting fragile sites from their visitors
paragraphs: Heritage sites face many threats, from war and neglect to pollution and climate change. But for some of the world's most famous places, the greatest pressure now comes from the people who love them most: their visitors. International travel has grown enormously over the past half century, helped by cheaper flights, rising incomes and, more recently, social media, which can turn a little-known beach or village into a global attraction almost overnight. For the managers of fragile sites, the challenge is to allow people to enjoy these places without destroying the very qualities that attract them.

Visitors can cause damage in ways that are not always obvious. Millions of footsteps wear away stone floors and steps, and erode paths on mountains and in national parks. In enclosed spaces, the warmth, moisture and carbon dioxide that people breathe out can change the air, encouraging the growth of algae and mould. Touching walls and statues leaves oils from the skin, and some visitors carve their names into ancient surfaces. Even the infrastructure built for tourists, such as car parks, hotels and souvenir shops, can spoil the setting of a site and place heavy demands on local water supplies.

One of the clearest examples of this kind of damage is the cave of Lascaux in south-west France. Its walls are covered with paintings of horses, deer and bulls, created around seventeen thousand years ago. After four teenagers discovered the cave in 1940, it was opened to the public, and by the late 1950s, more than a thousand people a day were visiting. Their breath and body heat changed the conditions inside the cave, and green algae began to grow on the paintings. In 1963, the cave was closed to the public, and it has remained closed ever since. Instead, visitors can see detailed replicas, the first of which opened nearby in 1983.

Few sites can simply be closed, however, so managers have developed other ways of controlling numbers. Many now require visitors to book tickets for a specific time. At Machu Picchu, the fifteenth-century Inca citadel in Peru, the authorities have introduced timed entry tickets, a daily limit on visitors and set routes through the site, so that people move in one direction rather than crowding into the most popular spots. Some visitors complain that these rules reduce their freedom, but they have made it possible to keep the site open while reducing wear on its stone terraces and stairways.

In some cases, a temporary closure has given nature a chance to recover. Maya Bay, on the Thai island of Ko Phi Phi Leh, became world famous after it appeared in the film The Beach, released in 2000. By the 2010s, thousands of visitors were arriving every day by boat, and the coral reef in the bay had been badly damaged by anchors, pollution and trampling. In 2018, the Thai authorities closed the bay completely. When it reopened in 2022, swimming was banned, boats were no longer allowed to enter the bay itself, and the number of visitors was limited. Scientists have reported that the coral is recovering and that sharks have returned to the shallow water.

Another approach is to use price to manage demand. The Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan has long followed a policy it describes as high value, low volume, which means attracting fewer visitors who each spend more, rather than large numbers of budget travellers. Most international visitors must pay a daily sustainable development fee, which is used to fund projects such as conservation and free healthcare. Critics argue that such fees make travel a privilege of the wealthy, but supporters say they ensure that tourism pays for its true costs, which are usually borne by local people and the environment.

Technology is also playing a growing role. Some sites now use sensors to count visitors in real time and adjust entry accordingly, while apps can suggest less crowded times or alternative attractions. Detailed digital models, created using laser scanning, allow people to explore places they could never visit in person, such as the interiors of fragile tombs. These tools cannot replace the experience of standing in front of a real monument, but they can reduce pressure on the most vulnerable sites and help to preserve a record of them in case they are damaged in the future.

Ultimately, managing visitors is not only about protecting stones and paintings; it is also about the people who live in and around heritage sites. Residents may benefit from tourism jobs, but they also experience rising rents, crowded streets and the loss of local shops to souvenir stalls. Successful management therefore requires their involvement in decisions. As one principle of sustainable tourism puts it, a place that is good to live in is usually also a good place to visit. The reverse, sadly, is not always true.

readingPassages.title: Should lost heritage be rebuilt?
paragraphs: When a great historic building is destroyed, whether by war, fire or deliberate attack, the first reaction is often a determination to rebuild it exactly as it was. Yet among conservation specialists, reconstruction has long been a controversial idea. A rebuilt monument, critics argue, is not the original but a copy, and treating a copy as if it were the real thing risks deceiving the public and devaluing genuine historic fabric. Others reply that buildings matter not only as old materials but as symbols of identity, and that rebuilding them can help communities to recover from trauma.

The modern conservation movement has generally been cautious. The Venice Charter, an influential international agreement drawn up by architects and conservation experts in 1964, states that restoration should be based on firm evidence and must stop where guesswork begins. Any new work needed should be clearly recognisable as modern, so that nobody confuses it with the original. Behind this approach lies a belief, developed in nineteenth-century Europe, that a building's value comes largely from its authentic materials and the marks that time has left on them.

Nevertheless, some of the most celebrated reconstructions of the twentieth century were made in direct contradiction to this principle. During the Second World War, most of the historic centre of Warsaw was deliberately destroyed by German forces. After the war, Polish architects rebuilt the old town's streets, churches and market square, using pre-war drawings and photographs, as well as eighteenth-century paintings of the city by the Italian artist Bernardo Bellotto. In 1980, the rebuilt centre was added to the World Heritage List, not as an original medieval town, but as an outstanding example of an almost complete reconstruction.

A similar story can be told about the Old Bridge at Mostar, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The elegant stone arch was completed in 1566 under Ottoman rule and stood for more than four centuries, until it was destroyed during the war in 1993. After the conflict, an international team rebuilt it using traditional methods, and divers recovered some of the original stones from the river below. The bridge reopened in 2004 and was added to the World Heritage List the following year. For many people, its reconstruction was a symbol of reconciliation between communities that had been on opposite sides of the war.

In Dresden, the eighteenth-century Frauenkirche, a Protestant church with a great stone dome, collapsed after the bombing of the city in 1945. For decades its ruins were left as a war memorial. Reconstruction began in 1994 and was completed in 2005, and wherever possible, original stones recovered from the ruins were put back in their former positions. Because the old stones are darkened by fire and age, the rebuilt church shows a pattern of dark and light stone, making the history of its destruction visible. In my view, this honest display of old and new is the most convincing answer to the charge that reconstruction is a form of deception.

Not every case of destruction has led to rebuilding. In 2001, the two giant Buddha statues carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan valley of Afghanistan, which had stood for around fifteen hundred years, were blown up by the Taliban. Since then, there has been a long debate about whether they should be reconstructed. Some argue that rebuilding would undo an act of cultural violence; others believe that the empty niches have become an important memorial in their own right, and that a reconstruction based on limited evidence would be largely imaginary. So far, the niches remain empty.

Perhaps the most interesting challenge to the Western emphasis on original materials comes from Japan. The Grand Shrine of Ise, one of the most sacred sites of the Shinto religion, has been rebuilt every twenty years for well over a thousand years, most recently in 2013. Each time, a new shrine is built on a neighbouring site using fresh wood and traditional techniques, and the old one is taken down. Here, what is preserved is not the material but the form and the knowledge of how to build it. Recognition of this kind of thinking led to the Nara Document on Authenticity of 1994, which accepted that ideas of authenticity vary between cultures.

The question returned to public attention after the fire at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 2019, which destroyed its roof and its nineteenth-century spire. After some debate about whether to add a modern design, the French authorities decided to rebuild the spire as it had been, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024. I believe that this was the right decision, because the spire had become part of how people around the world picture Paris. Reconstruction, in short, should not be rejected on principle. It should, however, be honest about what is new, and it should reflect the wishes of the people for whom the building has meaning.
